items.title: The Surprisingly Strange History of Ice Cream | Compilation
items.description:
I Scream! You Scream! We all scream for  ICE CREAM! We all know it, we all LOVE it! It has a long and storied history from its first creation to the incredible amount of variations that we can eat today! Come with us as we dive into all things ice cream! What is your favorite flavor? What is your best memory eating ice cream? Let us know in the comments! 

Chapters:
00:00:00 - The Death Of The Ice Cream Parlor
00:11:43 - The Well-Deserved Death Of The Ice Cream Truck
00:22:56 - The Ice Cold Deat
items.why_watch: This compilation traces ice cream from its aristocratic origins — when harvesting and storing ice was a luxury industry unto itself — through the industrial and cultural shifts that made it a democratic pleasure. At 83 minutes it's a genuine deep dive, better suited to a lazy Sunday afternoon than a quick break. If you've ever wondered why so many ice cream origin stories feel contradictory, this is where the threads get untangled.

items.title: A Very Odd Gangster: Monk Eastman
items.channel_title: The History Guy: History Deserves to Be Remembered
items.description:
Like the city that was his home, Monk Eastman was a study in contradictions.  At one point he kept five hundred pigeons, and by some estimates more than 100 cats. He loved bicycles so much that cronies would rent them just to curry his favor. And he would kill a person for $100.

items.why_watch: Monk Eastman was one of New York's most feared gang leaders around 1900, yet he kept hundreds of pigeons and cats and was fiercely loyal to his bicycle-riding friends — details that make him genuinely strange rather than just menacing. The History Guy specializes in exactly this kind of figure: historically significant but somehow left out of the standard curriculum. In 16 minutes you'll come away with a vivid portrait of Gilded Age street power and one very contradictory man.

items.title: Josh James NZ travel VLOG #370 Duckshooting, deer hunt, Wanganui Inlet and some other stuff
items.channel_title: Josh James KiwiBushman hunting fishing bushcraft
items.description:
Bit scattered this VLOG, had a few challenges and some ups and downs, thats life, but still managed to scrape together some content for your perusal!

 Whats been the highlight of your day?
items.why_watch: Josh James is refreshingly unpolished — he admits upfront this vlog is scattered and imperfect, which paradoxically makes the New Zealand backcountry footage feel more authentic than most outdoor content. The Wanganui Inlet scenery alone justifies the watch, and the mix of duck shooting and deer hunting gives a honest look at how subsistence-style hunting actually fits into everyday rural NZ life. Worth it if you like outdoor content that doesn't oversell itself.

discovery_articles.title: Art Exhibits at OAX Airport in San Juan Bautista la Raya, Mexico
discovery_articles.snippet: The state of Oaxaca in Mexico's south is often considered one of the country's main artistic hubs. Its diversity in nature and indigenous cultures has created an atmosphere of inspiration for creative endavors. In the capital city of the same name, known fully as Oaxaca de Juárez , perhaps the clearest examples are its booming gastronomic and graphic arts scenes.

discovery_articles.title: Papier-Mâché Altarpiece at Plaza Capuchinas in Mexico City, Mexico
discovery_articles.snippet: Cartonería is one of the main forms of artes populares (folk art), also known as artesanías (handcrafts), to come out of Mexico City and its metropolitan area. The terms refers to cartón, what cardboard is called in Mexican Spanish, and cartonería works use a type of papier-mâché technique for their building. Cartonería is the original medium for judas (figures intended to be burned at celebrations) and alebrijes , and a yearly event called La Noche de los Alebrijes takes place in Mexico City, in which monumental figures are paraded and displayed.

discovery_articles.title: Antimonumentas and Antimonumentos in Mexico City, Mexico
discovery_articles.snippet: Considering that Mexican cities have been ranked among the ones with highest homicide rates, a large number of massacres committed by organized crime groups as well as human rights violations by authorities, the last century or so has been rough for Mexico. In this context, the country's civilian population has often taken matters into their own hands regarding self-defense and demands towards the government. This is where the multitude of antimonuments mainly found in the capital come in.

discovery_articles.title: Ahuehuete del Centenario in Monterrey, Mexico
discovery_articles.snippet: On 20 September 1596, Spanish colonist Don Diego de Montemayor founded the city of Nuestra Señora (Our Lady) of Monterrey, in honor of Gaspar de Zúñiga y Acevedo, Viceroy of Mexico at the time and who was also the Count of Monterrey. The settlement was intended to become the capital of the "New Kingdom of León" after the Spanish region. To date, the city has come to be known simply as Monterrey and it remains the capital of what is now the Mexican state of Nuevo León, it also anchors what in the early 2020s became the country's second most-populated metropolitan area (with Metro Mexico City at a very distant first place).
